1:
Eight voices open this psalm, most with its plan. John Calvin sets it out: the writer calls on all creatures above and below, beginning with angels and passing to the brute creation and the dumb elements, then coming to men as the appointed heralds of praise, and at the close appealing to the children of Israel as principal witnesses, the unbelieving being blind to his works and dumb to his praises. He adds that Milton imitated the psalm and gave it to Adam and Eve as their morning hymn in innocency. Adam Clarke calls it the most sublime hymn of praise in the whole book, notes that it has no title though one old version attributes it to two prophets, and explains that the phrase from the heavens takes in all their inhabitants, as the answering phrase does of earth. Keil and Delitzsch ground the call in the honour God has bestowed on his people now that they are gathered out of exile and their city is risen from its ruins; they observe that the hymn of the three in the furnace, interpolated in the Greek text of another book, largely imitates this psalm, and that in the liturgy it bears the name of Laudes.

Augustine of Hippo takes the psalm as a discipline for this life. The subject of our meditation now should be the praises of God, since the exaltation of the life hereafter will be praise, and none becomes fit for that life who has not practised for it here; our praise is marked by joy and our prayer by groans, and the two seasons of the church year signify the tribulation we are in and the rest we hope for, one kept in fasting, the other in praises. C.H. Spurgeon presses the summons instead: whoever hears is invited, entreated and commanded to magnify the Lord, and those nearest the High and lofty One should lead the song, letting their worship fall like a golden shower on men beneath. No place is too high for the praises of the most High, he says, since the summit of creation shows his glory as the highest Alps are tipped with the sun that gladdens the valleys; and he counts the word praise sounding nine times in the first five verses.

Matthew Henry admits a difficulty. That angels are God’s hosts is plain, but what is meant by a man on earth exciting them to praise God he does not find easy to account for; he says only that it is God’s glory to have such attendants and more his glory that he neither needs them nor can be benefited by them, and that while we are cold and often interrupted, there are those above who do it better and rest not day nor night. Charles Ellicott attends to the grammar, allowing that some would render the opening as ye of the heavens but preferring the received version on the parallelism, since heavens and heights, like angels and hosts, are analogous pairs with the larger term last, so that the burst of praise comes from a choir in the heights.

The heaven of heavens draws most comment. Clarke expands it into systems of systems, reaching as far beyond the solar system as that reaches beyond the lowest deeps, and takes the waters above for clouds and rain and snow. Ellicott says the invocation pauses here to gather all the heights before descending to the earth, and explains the world of water as what Hebrew cosmology set upon the firmament. Clarke also states the principle behind addressing things without speech, that every work of God’s hand partakes so much of his perfections that it needs only study to show forth his wisdom. John Gill makes the sun and moon praise God by doing the work appointed them and giving men cause to praise him for their light and warmth.
5:
The reason for praising the heavens is the decree that fixed them, and Charles Ellicott presses the wording. He renders the verb as making to stand, and takes the second clause to say that God has made an ordinance and will not transgress it, not that the creatures do not. The line anticipates, but only in form, the modern doctrine of the inviolability of natural order, since what makes the law invariable is the faithfulness of God; and he cites two prophetic passages supposing a covenant between God and nature as with his people. He adds that the received English rendering, which follows two old versions in making the ordinance itself imperishable, violates the usage of the verb. Adam Clarke takes the creating word as the utterance of an idea in the infinite mind, and reads the establishing as the fixing of their revolutions, so that they have never passed the line marked out nor intercepted one another in the vortex of space. John Gill applies it to the angels, made immortal and confirmed in their happiness, and John Wesley says they are constant and incorruptible, not changeable like the things below.

At the call to the earth Matthew Henry pauses. This earth and its atmosphere, he says, are the very sediment of the universe, and it concerns us to find what reconciles us to a place in it; next to the visit the Son of God made here, he knows nothing better than that even in this dark world God is praised. As the sun’s rays are darted from heaven and reflected back more weakly, so should the praises of God be, with which this cold and infected world is to be warmed and perfumed. Clarke fills the deep with whales and sharks, whirlpools and ground tides and the astonishing flux and reflux of the ocean, holding that everything in its place shows forth the perfections of its Creator. Ellicott notes that the invocation now passes downwards and that the first sound of earthly praise comes, by the order of the creation story, from the sea-monsters, the deeps added to take in all great waters.

The powers of the air draw Ellicott’s longest note. The fire is lightning; the word rendered vapours means smoke elsewhere and is connected with burning, so that the four terms may form a chiasmus, the smoke answering to the fire as the snow to the hail; yet the driving mists of a storm are also treated as smoke, and he quotes a modern poet on smoky mountain tops. He calls this summons a fine poetic touch showing how freely the lyric handles the story of creation, which passes at once from the monsters of the deep to the land, whereas the poet finds another region of life whose voices, wild as they are, may join the anthem; and the stormy wind, seemingly free and uncontrollable, is only a messenger fulfilling the word given it. Gill supplies histories, the lightning that consumed the cities of the plain and the hail that was one of the plagues and slew the Canaanites. Clarke ranges over the air in all its forms, breeze and gale and whirlwind and tempest and tornado, each accomplishing a particular will of the Most High.

On the mountains and trees Clarke turns geologist, taking in hills primitive, secondary and alluvial with their quarries and mines, and exclaiming at the wisdom lavished on them, especially on precious stones; the varied hues and savours of fruit, he adds, proclaim the same wisdom as the uses of the forest trees. Ellicott follows the movement of the psalm, which alights on the crests of the highest mountains and passes down to the lower hills where vegetable life begins, and divides the trees between the fruit-bearing kinds men plant and the cedars, of God’s own planting. Gill adds the gold and silver and iron the hills contain.
10:
The animals give Adam Clarke his opening. He sorts them, wild beasts, domestic animals kept for house and field, then the whole class of reptiles, which he measures from the boa constrictor that can kill and swallow whole a royal tiger down to a poisonous creature no thicker than a needle, and beyond these to the animals in water that only a microscope brings into view, in all of which, he says, is a profusion of wisdom that would take ages to exhibit. The birds hold him longest: their structure is astonishing, and the exact mathematical manner in which they swim the air and steer their course, with the feathers and the muscles that move them, strikes the observer with astonishment and delight. Charles Ellicott keeps to the arrangement, the wild set against the domesticated and the creeping things against the birds that fly above them, while John Gill adds that the beasts wait on God for their food and so praise him.

When the psalm reaches mankind the order is remarked on. Gill observes that the order of creation is kept throughout, so that man, made last, is called on last and the chief among men first; kings have cause to praise God, since promotion comes not by chance but from him who sets up kings and puts them down. Clarke takes the ranks in turn, kings as representatives of the Most High, princes as governors of provinces and judges as executing the laws that preserve civil society, and asks the people to magnify God for those institutions and the laws that keep their lives and properties. Ellicott marks a change of role: the whole universe having been summoned, man takes his place as leader of the choir, in language framed to include all ranks and nations, of every age and each sex. On the young and the old Clarke pairs the ends of life as very appropriately united, since the beginning and the conclusion present nearly the same passions and infirmities, and in both the sustaining power of God is seen; the young, he says, should give the morning of their days. Gill divides the praise, the young men for their strength and the maidens for their beauty.

At the close the interest is all in the last verse. Ellicott renders it that God has raised a horn for his people, takes this to imply some victory, or the assurance of one, which he supposes prompted the song, and then answers a charge brought against the verse. It has been said to narrow a grand universal anthem into an anti-climax; but while poetically the whole universe can be called to sing the hallelujah, the thing itself remains what it always was, the covenant privilege of one people, and on that view the objection falls. Gill makes the horn an emblem of power and dominion and reports the reading that finds Christ in it, and John Wesley that the word denotes strength, victory, glory and felicity. Ellicott also corrects excellent to exalted in the thirteenth verse, and finds a fine artistic touch in the order of its words, since all heaven and earth are summoned to the chorus of one then declared to be above earth and heaven.

Clarke ends with a peroration rather than a note. What a hymn of praise is here, he exclaims, a universal chorus in which all created nature has a share, and man particularly in all the stages of his being. God loves man wherever found, of whatever colour and in whatever circumstances, at every stage of his pilgrimage from the cradle to the grave; so let the lisp of the infant, the shout of the adult and the sigh of the aged ascend as one gratitude-offering to him who guards those that hang upon the breast, controls the headstrong and giddy, and sustains old age under its infirmities.
